tip: Yes/no questions put the verb first: wil je koffie? is literally want you coffee, with je after the verb.
klaar means ready or finished, not clear: het avondeten is bijna klaar = dinner is almost ready.
nooit means never and already carries the negation, so you add no separate niet: ik vergeet nooit.
graag after a verb says you like doing it: zij danst graag = she likes to dance.
dragen means both to wear and to carry: zij draagt een jurk = she wears a dress.
luisteren takes naar for what you listen to: luisteren naar de radio = listen to the radio.
The ending -in makes a noun female: vriend is a male friend, vriendin a female friend or girlfriend.
Illnesses use hebben with no article: koorts hebben = to have a fever, literally have fever.
To ask the time, Dutch says hoe laat is het?, literally how late is it?
Dutch often uses the perfect where English uses simple past: we hebben je gemist = we missed you.
Before a de-word with een, the adjective adds -e: een blauwe jas, since jas is a de-word.
As a position word, door means through: de hond rent door de tuin = through the garden.
zal marks the future and pushes the main verb to the end: ik zal het boek morgen terugbrengen.
In the perfect tense the past participle moves to the end: hij heeft het boek niet gelezen.
With a time word like morgen, Dutch uses the present for future events: ik ga morgen = I am going tomorrow.
A het-word with een keeps the adjective bare: een nieuw huis, because huis is a het-word.
schoonmaken is a separable verb; in a main clause it splits: ik maak het huis schoon.
elke means every and is followed by a singular noun: elke zomer = every summer.
The ending -je makes a diminutive: plaat becomes plaatje = little picture.
Use deze with de-words and dit with het-words: deze week, because week is a de-word.
Dutch uses the present with al for something still going on: de regen valt al = it has been raining.
With a separable verb, te sits between the two parts: op te staan, from opstaan = to get up.
Nouns ending in a single vowel add apostrophe-s in the plural: collega becomes collega's.
net means just now or recently: het ziekenhuis is net gerenoveerd = just renovated.
nicht means both niece and female cousin; context decides which: mijn nicht studeert.
After the definite het, the adjective takes -e: het vegetarische gerecht.
A few nouns form the plural with -eren: kind becomes kinderen = children.
goed has an irregular comparative: beter = better, not goeder.
The set phrase for how are you is hoe gaat het met...?, literally how goes it with.
thuis means at home on its own, with no preposition: ik knip mijn haar thuis.
Compounds join two words and the last one sets the meaning: voor plus tuin = voortuin, front garden.
gelijk hebben means to be right, literally to have right: hij heeft gelijk.
gaan plus an infinitive expresses the near future: zij gaat een baan zoeken = she is going to look.
nog steeds means still, for something that keeps going: wonen nog steeds = still live.
het plus an infinitive works as a noun, like the -ing form: het hardlopen = running.
Dutch says the units before the tens: vijfentwintig is five-and-twenty = 25.
na means after in time: na de verkiezing = after the election.
huren is to rent from someone; renting out is the opposite verb verhuren: hij huurt een auto.
Days of the week take op: op vrijdag = on Friday.
achter means behind: achter het huis = behind the house.
vanaf means from a starting point: vanaf de brug = from the bridge.
tijdens means during: tijdens de vergadering = during the meeting.
Before a plural noun the adjective always takes -e: verse sinaasappelen.
When introducing people, dit stays singular even before a plural: dit zijn mijn buren.
next or last plus a time unit needs no preposition: volgende maand = next month.
